utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, before we start with the next witness, the Trial Chamber is seized with the Prosecution's motion to preclude two Defence witnesses and the Prosecution refers to the quality of the Rule 65 ter filing with regard to these witnesses. We would like to hear from both parties on this issue. We might spend about 20 minutes on that. Since this motion is filed by the Prosecution, we would like to hear the Prosecution first. Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. I will indeed be brief. It's our position or the position that we take on this issue is found in the written submissions that we made, Mr. President. I think there is very little to add. Beyond what I think is simply a reassertion of the position that we have asserted ever since the Defence first began submitting witness summaries under Rule 65. Our position has always been, both in written submissions and oral submissions to the Trial Chamber at various times since the proceedings began, that the summaries are insufficient and do not satisfy the terms of the Rule. Now, I looked again at the Rule this morning, Mr. President, 65 ter (G). The Rule requires both parties, including the Defence, to provide a summary of the facts on which each witness will testify, the facts. It's our position, Mr. President, that the summaries that have been filed and continue to be filed by the Defence, because there have been a series of summaries that have been filed in different forms over the last three weeks or so. The summaries provided do not contain a summary of the facts; they contain a summary of the issues or the topics, I think read generously to the Defence. We are getting a list of the topics, general idea of the subject matter, but we are not getting the facts. And that is the basic crux of our submission, and the point on which we argue that the summaries are insufficient under the letter of the Rule. Now, with respect to the two witnesses who are subject of this motion, and just out of an abundance of caution I won't name them. I don't think it's necessary. I think they are both public or so far intend to testify publicly but it's not necessary I think to identify them. And this goes partially to the assertion by the Defence that this motion is filed too late or that we somehow went along for two or three weeks without having expressed any objections and now here at the last moment comes the Prosecution with this motion, and it's too late. What the Defence response fails to point out is that there has since been a subsequent submission by the Defence dated the 4th of April. The two most recent summaries filed by the Defence are filed on the 21st of March, and then most recently on the 4th of April. If you look at these two witnesses, and the manner in which their summaries change, what you find is that with Witness Z, I call him Witness Z, the most recent filing contains even less information than the previous filing. That's number 1. Secondly, the time envisioned for his direct testimony increases from one hour to two and a half hours. So in the most recent submission, not referred to by the Defence in their response, we see now that this witness is going to testify 2 and a half hours on direct instead of one hour, while at the same time, there is even less information contained in the most recent summary than was contained in the earlier summary of 21 March. And that's the same for Witness K. His testimony goes from one and a half now to three hours on direct, as indicated in the most recent witness summary filed the 4th of April, and yet again, his witness summary contains less information than that contained in the earlier summary. So that's a new fact, and it's something that we think is -- one of the reasons why we felt it necessary to bring this motion to the Trial Chamber's attention at this time. Secondly, I think in terms of new information or new facts, why did we wait? We've now been through three Defence witnesses. We've been in a position for our part, Mr. President, to gauge the extent to which the summaries were being provided are of any use in preparing a meaningful cross-examination and after having seen three Defence witnesses come and go, I think I can say with confidence on behalf of the Prosecution, that the summaries being provided do not provide any assistance, or the sort of assistance that we are entitled to under the Rule. And so, those are two factors which have led us to believe that it was necessary to file this motion at the time that we did. And beyond that, Mr. President, I can -- I don't think I have anything more to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I have two questions to you. The first one is that if indeed it is too late to file that motion at this stage, I understand that those two witnesses are the fourth of six witnesses in the order provided by Defence counsel for time. If you have any objections, we believe that you have to leave some time for the response from Defence counsel. I'm still not very clear why don't you move a little bit earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, maybe my perception is wrong. I think we've attempted to express our objections to the summaries at various points along the way. The Defence at one point said, "Well, why do not you choose the ones that you think are insufficient and we'll see about trying to remedy that." I think it's our position that we shouldn't be put in that position of choosing, picking and choosing, among the summaries. The Rule entitles us to a summary of facts. We are not getting facts for any witness. And we would resist being put in a position of having to select those for whom we would like greater information when in fact it's our view that the summaries don't comply with the Rule; any of them. I understand that the timing of this motion raises difficulties if in fact the witnesses are here. All I can say, Mr. President, like I've said already, is that the most recent filing of summaries dated the 4th of April is one in which we are seeing greater testimony time for these witnesses at the same time that the summaries are becoming shorter. And also, it's become clear to us after these first three witnesses that the summaries that we've gotten simply aren't satisfactory. We can't work with them. They put us in a very difficult situation in attempting to conduct a cross. We've tried to go along as best we can with what we've got but I think the trend based on what we've seen today and based upon the information that appears to be getting smaller in the summaries, the trend is what led us to file this motion at the time that we filed it, recognising that it does raise logistical difficulties in respect of witnesses who are in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. The second question is, you asked the Trial Chamber to move to preclude two witnesses. I would like to know on what legal basis should the Trial Chamber act? I believe in your filings, you have to indicate or invoke the specific Articles in the Rules of Procedures. We found that there are two Rules that seem to be applicable, that is the Rule 65 ter (N), and the Rule 68 bis. We believe that in the later filings, if you ask us to do something, you have to indicate at least the legal basis for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Point well taken, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You still did not answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think that clearly both of those Rules supply the legal basis for excluding evidence. It's not clear to me, Mr. President, that we've gotten -- well, I think in order to get to that point, the Trial Chamber first has to make a finding as to whether the summaries provided satisfy the terms of Rule 65 ter (G), whether we are getting a summary of facts, and if, in fact, the Trial Chamber concludes that these summaries do not comply with the Rule, which I don't believe we have gotten to that point yet with the Trial Chamber, if you so find, then clearly, 65 ter (N) and 68 bis provide the basis for them taking the next step which is to exclude the testimony or to provide other remedies. And on this point, Mr. President, let me say excluding the witnesses from testifying entirely is certainly a remedy that in our view could be justified. However, there are other remedies possible, such as postponing cross-examination, bringing the witnesses back for cross-examination at a later time, which would enable us to more effectively prepare a cross-examination. So there are other remedies that fall short of the most severe remedy of exclusion but we think that based on the witnesses, the summaries, and the situation that we are being increasingly placed in, we think that exclusion is something that the Trial Chamber is going to have to consider if we are not supplied with summaries that in our view comply with the Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. May I turn to Mr. Krsnik? Mr. Meek, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We want to hear your response to this motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes. I will respond to my learned colleague. First, Your Honour, I believe that I want to make it absolutely clear that the filing on April 4th was only to increase the hours. The Defence believed after the first witness and the commencement of the second witness on the 2nd of April, that we had miscalculated on the hours that we had put down. The hours were, as you know, on these two witnesses who are in question, modified and it was only out of an abundance of caution that we increased the possible hours for direct examination. I will tell the Court, the Trial Chamber, that we do not intend to use any more than the originally allotted time but we believed in good faith that it would be better to err on the side of caution when it came to informing the Trial Chamber of how many hours we intended on direct examination. In regards to the motion itself, I will agree with Your Honours that the Prosecution did not state a basis in their motion as to what Rule they relied upon, and further, Your Honours, I will -- would like to point out that the key factor in the argument of the Prosecution seems to be that they are looking for witness summaries which will comply with what they believe -- their view of what the Rule encompasses. This, Your Honours, puts the Defence into a situation of never being able to make the Prosecution happy. If we come back and make supplements to our 65 ter rulings on summaries, there is absolutely nothing to stop the Prosecution from coming back with another motion, yet another motion, yet another motion. I do not believe, Your Honours, that the Prosecution, and I believe the Trial Chamber can adequately and amply see that during the first three witnesses the Defence has called, and these three witnesses have been completed, that the right of the cross-examination by the Prosecution has not been hindered in any fashion. The Trial Chamber has granted extra time for the cross-examination. There has been no objection on the Defence to some extra time for cross-examination over the amount of direct examination. And there is one thing I would like to say, Your Honours in regards to Mr. Stringer's argument. My learned colleague indicated to you just now orally that we had approached them and talked with the Prosecution team and indicated to them that -- asked them to point out which ones they believed were not sufficient in regards to witness summaries. And Your Honours, we met in good faith on the 20th of March, in the morning, prior to the Pre-Defence Conference to talk about this very same subject. Upon a question to the Prosecution team, which is, "Do you maintain that each and every witness summary that we have filed under 65 ter is insufficient?" The answer was no. The question that was specifically asked to the Prosecution team on that day: "If you will point out one, two, or three, or four summaries you believe are sufficient, then we will know what standard you believe we need to meet to make you happy." They will think about it, was the answer. They will get back to us, was the answer. We haven't heard that. We didn't ask for them to go through every one and say which ones were insufficient. We wanted to know whether they believed all were insufficient. They said no, they didn't believe all were insufficient. So all we asked for was a couple of examples and then we would try to help them with their wishes. That never came about. We are still very open to that possibility. And we will be happy to meet with them at any time to give them more information. We believe, Your Honours, that this motion is filed at such a late hour that we have now no possibility -- well, actually we do have a possibility of informing the Prosecution team, either orally, which I believe would be probably more appropriate, and I think Mr. Seric, these are joint witnesses by the way, these are joint witnesses, they are not witnesses to the actual Counts against either of the accused. They are witnesses to general allegations, background and international armed conflict. We, as stated in the motion or response, Your Honours, we stand by the filings, we believe that they are adequate, we believe that the Prosecution is not prejudiced whatsoever. We believe that the Honourable Trial Chamber can see from the cross-examination that the Prosecution has made with the last three defence witnesses, that they are more than up to the task of cross-examining our witnesses with the abundance of evidence, documents, staff that they have at their fingertips, and we believe that they are not prejudiced. Since this is a joint witness, Mr. Seric is also I believe going to address the Court briefly and Mr. Seric can certainly answer any questions more fully than I can in regards to the substance of the proposed testimony of these two witnesses. We do, Your Honour, stand by the fact that we only added the time on April 4th in those filings out of an abundance of caution. We do not believe that the direct examination will take any longer than is originally envisioned. We believe, Your Honours, that granting this motion would cause irreparable damage and prejudice to the Defence of both Mr. Naletilic and Mr. Martinovic. We believe that it would be unfair to have a direct examination, send these witnesses back home to have them return in a week or two weeks while they are still under oath. And Your Honours, I'm not going to take up much more of your time but we do not believe, like the Prosecution believes or appears to believe, that they have set some standard for this Tribunal on 65 ter filings. And we are wondering, no matter what we do, how can we satisfy the Prosecution? So we don't want to be caught in a catch-22 situation where we file separately and we get the same response we have now, and that is it's not good enough. Your Honours, with all due respect, we respectfully request that the Prosecution's motions be denied and I believe Mr. Seric would like to address the Court briefly. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise. My mike was not on. I'll repeat. Good morning, Your Honours. I will be very brief since we are limited in time. I endorse everything mentioned by Mr. Meek but I'd like to draw your attention to a fact which I'm of course sure that you are fully familiar with, much better than myself. As far as Rule 65 ter (N) is concerned, it stresses that upon a report of the Pre-Trial Judge, the Trial Chamber shall decide should the case arise on sanctions to be imposed on party and 65 ter (G) point B is particularly relevant here, a summary of the facts on which each witness will testify. We submitted the summaries of facts, obviously this has been covered. Now, whether the summaries are in coherence with the taste and expectations of the Prosecution, whether they contain all the facts that the Prosecution deems to be relevant is an arbitrary question. However, whether the sanctions under this Rule can -- it doesn't say that it will exclude preclusion of a witness's testimony. So the Trial Chamber may refer to exclusion as a remedy which we believe is the ultimate remedy to be imposed by the Trial Chamber. We believe, however, that this is not the case, and that Rule 68 bis is not relevant here. To conclude, Your Honours, we have the witnesses here. The witnesses are waiting to be examined. Therefore we believe that the wisest proposal for the future practice would be to meet again with the other party and to clarify the situation which we have now been brought into. Given the circumstances and the speed with which the proceedings have been proceeding and we apologise, Your Honours for bringing you in a situation in which you have to arbitrate in this manner. Both parties, the Defence and the Prosecution, in our view, could have resolved this situation without your being involved but we would humbly plead with you not to exclude our witness. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let me make two comments on the submissions from Mr. Meek. First of all, this Trial Chamber does not believe that efficient cross-examination is an excuse for you not to apply the 65 ter obligations. It is your obligation to file the summaries of the facts on which each witness will testify according to that Rule, no matter how the other side will conduct its cross-examination. Secondly, Mr. Meek, the standards for the sufficient summary of the facts, according to that Rule, lies in the Rule itself, rather than depends on the request from the other party, because you have to satisfy the Chamber that you performed your duty according to that Rule. That's all I want to say at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If I could offer two brief comments, Mr. President? Firstly, in our view, it's perhaps an issue or a question that's less subjective than the Defence has framed it and I think that it is possible from an objective point of view to distinguish between a list of facts or a summary of facts and simply a more generic summary of the topics without going into what they are going to it say about each of those topics, and as we move away from witnesses who come to it speak about the broader political issues in the case, as we get down to street level on the front line in Mostar, for example, when those witnesses start to come, it's even going to be a greater difficulty to cross-examine when we don't know what the facts are. My second comment is perhaps something that we could mention informally to the Defence, but if the witnesses are here, in this situation, is it possible we could consider having them each testify on direct, one after the other, and then come back to the cross-examination of the first one and then follow that with the cross-examination of the second one? It would give us a bit more time to prepare based on what is said in the direct, because in our view, the summary doesn't provide any meaningful information. So that if we were to do both of them on direct and then do both of them on cross, it would stagger things out a little bit, which may enable us to prepare to cross them more effectively rather than asking that they be sent home and come back at a later time. It's just something that I offer off the top of my head actually. I don't know how the Trial Chamber or the Defence would respond to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, this Trial Chamber will make its decisions this afternoon after deliberations. But at this point, I would like to mention certain issues concerning with the filings from the Defence counsel. During the proceedings and during the Pre-Trial, Pre-Defence Conference, this Trial Chamber mentioned several times -- asked for the timely and sufficient submission of the filings according to the Rule 65 ter. We are a little bit disappointed up to now, there is no sufficient filings according to that Rule. We hope that the Defence counsel could refile its summaries as soon as possible. In the meantime, I would like to remind the Defence counsel we need the full, summary of the facts, of the testimony by the expert witness, at least in two weeks' time; otherwise, we believe that this Trial Chamber will be in the position to preclude those expert witnesses. Having said that, we'll hear the next witness. Mr. Usher, would you please bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may sit down, please. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I should like to remind you at the outset of the following in view of the fact that we speak the same language and in order to facilitate the work of our very precious interpreters and for the best possible quality of the interpretation of what you say, have a look at the screen and try to follow the transcript on the screen, and when you see that the text has stopped, you may proceed with your answer. Thank you for allowing me to give you this warning. I think we can now start with a very brief introduction of yourself, Witness. That is if you could please tell us the place of birth, the date of birth, what kind of educational background you have and what you did up until 1990?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Your Honours, gentlemen, I'm Jozo Maric, I was born on the 5th of September, 1948, in Donji Amici, in the municipality of Grude in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And also I should like to ask you to speak slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: I completed my primary education in Grude in 1963. Thereafter, I left for Vinkovci which is in the Republic of Croatia where I completed my secondary education, the grammar school in 1967. In 1967, I enrolled in Sarajevo, in college for land surveying, which I completed in 1969. In 1970, I became a student of the Faculty of Philosophy at the literature and art history department in the town of Zadar. I obtained my degree from this university in 1974. And as early as the 1st of October, 1974, I started to work as a secondary school teacher in the town of Bugojno in the secondary technical school, school for engineering. I remained in the town of Bugojno until 1981 when I returned to Grude, where I continued to teach at the local grammar school. I taught literature and history of art. I was a secondary school professor or teacher until the first multi-party elections which took part in 1990. In the meantime, in 1978 and 1979, I took a course at the law school in Split. Having spent one year there, I enrolled in a masters programme at the University of Zagreb, where I majored in the so-called auxiliary historical sciences, and perhaps another point of interest, I completed my compulsory military service with the JNA in 1975-76 in the town of Pivka in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Witness. Let us move on. Again, I have to ask you to be very brief and tell the Court something about your political involvement since 1990. What kind of political activities you performed, what kind of positions you held, and so on and so forth, but please try to be very brief and I will lead you later on.

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: My political involvement does not start in 1990. It actually began as early as 1968 when in Sarajevo...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm really sorry to interrupt you, Witness. This is just for the purposes of introduction and that is why I'm interested only in the period of time following 1990. Later on, we can come back with the assistance of my questions.

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: In 1990, at the first democratic elections which were held on the 18th of November, I was elected a deputy to the municipal assembly in Grude. On the 3rd of December, 1990, during the first session of this assembly, I was elected president of the then Grude municipal assembly, the position I held until mid-1992, when I was elected president of the civilian section of the HVO. I did not hold this position for very long, only until autumn, 1992, when I became commissioner for the educational and physical educational department within the Croatian Community Herceg-Bosna. At the same time, I was acting president of the war prisoners exchange commission, between the warring parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but only insofar as the work pertained to the conflict between Serbs and Croats or Bosniaks. In that capacity, I participated in the winter of 1993 at the international conference of the ICRC in Geneva. The same year, 1993, when the Croatian government -- when the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was established I was elected Minister of Education, Culture, and Physical Education in that government, the position which I held up until the constitutional changes, that is, the beginning of the implementation of the Washington and Dayton Accords, when in 1996 I was elected president of the western Hercegovinian province. That is the president of the so-called Zupanija. Well, that would conclude my political activities until 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: After your introduction, I should like to begin with my actual examination, Witness. My first question would be as follows: Could you describe for us the way the government functioned in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: I'll be happy to do that. In 1992, despite the conflict that had already started in the area of the former Yugoslavia, in the territory of my municipality in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the local government behaved the same -- in the same manner as it did in 1990, that is, it was not faced with any major difficulties at the time. Unfortunately, after the outbreak of the conflict, that is the first hostilities in 1991 in the area of eastern Herzegovina, precisely in the village of Ravno, and with the arrival of the JNA and the Serbian and Montenegrin reservists, in the western hills of the Mostar area, we were forced to think about the future. That is, we were faced with a very serious question, what would happen if the so-called JNA moved on towards the municipalities of the western Herzegovina, including Grude? Their positions in Krusevo, for example, were less than 25 kilometres as the crow flies from Grude. Therefore, any serious artillery piece, such as the JNA obviously had, could have at any moment endangered the area by opening fire. Consequently, we had to take care of the security issues and the organisation of the defence, not only in our municipality but beyond our municipality as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Sorry once again for interrupting you. I would like to know, whether at that point in time, some organisations were established and did you participate in any such bodies of authority at the time? How did the government function at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had 107 or 108 municipalities. It was an unitary entity at the time. We did not change anything as far as the legal setup was concerned but there was an association at the time which was called the association of municipalities; it was an old political and administrative term. These associations functioned on a regional level. My municipality, the municipality of Grude, belonged to the so-called association of municipalities of the southern Herzegovina which also included municipalities such as Neum, Capljina, Citluk, Grude and Ljubuski. The president of these local municipalities, but also representatives of other service, very often conducted talks pertaining to the various problems that these municipalities were faced with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: When was HZ HB established and what were the reasons of its establishment?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: When we realised that the central government in Sarajevo was not taking any steps, faced with the danger which was not only present beyond the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina but could already be felt in -- inside Bosnia and Herzegovina in a very serious way -- let me just remind you of the month of October, and the destruction of the village of Ravno in the eastern Herzegovina and the expulsion of the Croatian population from that village, also the positions held by the JNA and the Serbian and Montenegrin reservists on the western bank of the Neretva River.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let me remind you once again of the need to speak slowly for the benefit of the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, faced with a danger of that kind, it was our belief that the reasons why we were elected to our positions was not -- were not only to organise every day life in normal conditions but that we were also required to prepare ourselves for the potentially necessary defence of these areas. In particular, in view of the fact that in the month of May, 1991, a huge column consisting of large number of tanks had passed in a rather threatening manner through the area of the western Herzegovina, I believe that this is something that you are aware of. The column was stopped at the outskirts of the town of Siroki Brijeg but was peacefully let go without any major incident. Once a promise had been made by them that they were going to an ordinary and normal military exercise, that that was the purpose of this passage. Unfortunately, nothing was ordinary any longer, which could be plainly seen from the deployment of the tank units in the area of Kupres. We were no longer allowed access to this area, which had before been common practice by the JNA, that is this kind of access in the past had been allowed. I as a soldier of the JNA, I participated in Slovenia in such military exercise, which could freely be attended by and observed by civilians, even children. So all these considerations, all these facts, were telling us that those were not normal military exercises, especially in view of what had already happened in Croatia and in view of the tragedy that had befallen the village of Ravno. So it was at that point in time that we started to think seriously about the defence of the population. It was then that we realised that there could not be any form of volunteerism as far as the defence is concerned, that in terms of defence, we could not count on the will of the people. We had recourse to the then constitutional possibilities in the then Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is the association of municipalities which I have described. We simply enlarged an administrative form, an administrative unit, which was already provided for legally. We were aware of the fact that the defence could not be organised in restricted areas, therefore, we established the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the basic characteristics of this type of association? Was it a state? Was it a form of government or authority? Was it provisional or temporary in nature? Could you briefly describe its nature?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Obviously it is possible to describe the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Its characteristics can be plainly seen from its founding document, one of them being the recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna took into account the overall Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, mention was also made of the need to take into account the extraordinary circumstances and the extraordinary situation and to organise everyday life in view of that. It was therefore an association which comprised the municipalities where Croats, according to the 1991 census, had majority or rather where they were the majority population. We had already observed that the central government in Sarajevo, at least this was our opinion, was rather naive in their belief that they or, rather, Bosnia and Herzegovina, would be spared by war. We, on the other hand, knew that what was going on in Croatia, what had happened in Vukovar and the village of Ravno, would only happen to us, but in a more serious way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, can you tell us, if you know, when the HVO was established and also describe for us the section of the HVO where you worked?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: The HVO was established on the 8th of April, 1992, after the so-called peace brigade, which we had peacefully let go in the spring of 1991, destroyed the municipality of Kupres and evicted its population. An incident in which hundreds of civilians from Kupres were killed and the rest expelled. So it was after this incident on the 8th of April, 1992, we believed that it was no longer possible for us to defend our areas in a non-organised, voluntary manner. We were faced with a very well-organised JNA. Accordingly, the defence had to be organised in accordance with all positive international regulations governing conflicts, defence and war in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you tell us what your function within the HVO was? And you also haven't told us -- I'm sorry. I have to interrupt you and lead you a little bit because your answers tend to be rather longish.

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Thank you. Immediately upon April the 8th, 1992, two HVOs were established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you please tell us the following? I cannot submit to you leading questions. Could you tell me what are the components and organisations within the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: This is what I was going to say. The HVO comprises two units, two components, the civilian and the defence, military component. I became president of the HVO in the municipality of Grude. In other words, this was the municipal government, consisting of the same people but operating under extraordinary wartime conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Which is the component in which you were active?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: I was involved in the civilian component.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What was your function?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: I was president -- I was president of the HVO of the Grude municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you tell us when, as testified by you before in front of this Tribunal, when do you start working in the HVO social affairs department? When do you get involved with sports, education, physical education and culture?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: It is only in autumn of 1992 that, upon the establishment of the civilian HVO, that is HZ HB, I became the head of the subdepartment for education, culture, and sports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So at that time, you became responsible for the area of education. Could you tell us what were the conditions under which schools were operating? Were schools open and working in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: No sooner had in April, 1992, an open and widespread offensive been launched by the JNA, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, from the area Posavina Bijeljina, further on to Kupres, Sarajevo, and when all the capabilities were used by the JNA to launch these attacks, and these did not only include the infantry and the artillery units but also the air force. Then we, for the sake of the safety and security of the children, and given the daily air attacks, decided to interrupt the instruction at school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: When was the school year interrupted, in which month to be specific? And when was the work of the schools resumed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, is that a relevant question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it is relevant because we are now entering the most relevant part that has to do with the direct examinations by the learned friend. We are entering now the most important matters about the HZ HB, the organisation of education and training system, and everything that goes with that, i.e., the right to use one's mother tongue, the teachers, the professors, whether they were expelled or not. These are the matters that we are now entering, the HZ HB now is already a fact, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, there is only three matters, major matters, we want to hear from this witness. First, the internal structure of the HVO, as the witness testified just now, there are two sections, two components of the HVO. One is military, the other is civilian. This witness told us that he held a position in the civilian part of the HVO. That's what we want to hear. Secondly, is that the life in Mostar during the period from 1992 to 1993? Thirdly, the witness told us that he was in charge of the exchanging of detainees between the parties. This is the three aspects we want to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, certainly, all the three topics mentioned by you will be covered, but the prisoners of war is the situation somewhere in 1999 -- beginning of 1993. This is not the situation from May, 1992 onward. However, the witness will certainly describe these aspects as well for Their Honours to be able to get a full picture. Your Honours, we are following the indictment. This witness was a professor, was a teacher. We heard about the expulsions of the professors. We heard about the difficulties concerning the use of their mother tongue. This witness was the Minister of Education and it seems to me that we invited the most meritorious witness and this, Your Honours, is also one of the counts of the indictments and it is not my fault that I have to respond to all the counts of the indictment. Of course, I will certainly bear in mind that the three major topics you outlined need to be focused. You also know, Your Honours, that we were tendered statements and testimonies made by an incompetent witness who was a mufti in Mostar and through this witness, the learned friend made an attempt to paint the picture and now the Defence is trying to shed a few shreds of truth on that -- to that picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed, but as concise as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very briefly in two sentences, when was the school year interrupted and when was it resumed?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: The school year 1991-92 was interrupted mainly at the beginning of April of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And when was the school work resumed?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: The usual start of a school year, which was September, was delayed but we still did resume the work of the schools in September, and it went on until the new year of 1993. Given the wartime situation, given the expelled population, the refugees, and given the destroyed school buildings, unfortunately some schools never resumed with their work, and I'm referring to the period under discussion here. This could not be done because people were expelled and because some areas were occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you tell us what was the curriculum and the programme in schools and let us now, from now onward, focus only upon the year 1992. Where could the curriculum and the programme be implemented and how did they look like?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: For the sake of the whole truth, I should describe in a sentence or two the curricula and programmes in the former Yugoslavia. The curricula and the school programmes in the former Yugoslavia were practically identical, regardless of the fact that the drafting of the curricula and programmes was within the authority of the governments of the former republics. In other words, the former Yugoslavia's school system, it is a universally known fact, was a centralised one, and as far as these curricula and programmes are concerned, we changed nothing in the school year 1991-92. In the school year 1992-93, we continued with the implementation of the same curricula, the same programme. However, an intervention was made within the curriculum and the programme in terms of de-idealisation of the curriculum and the programmes, i.e., stripping them of the communist elements that they had contained. The only one more radical change made was the elimination of the subject titled "defence and protection" and that at the level of the secondary schools only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, could you please focus a bit more in your answers? Of course, you are not quite sure what we are particularly interested in. However, let us not confuse this Tribunal. Therefore, let us focus upon that aspect of the curriculum and the programme of the mother tongue in 1992-93, 1993 and 1994 school years. I will therefore proceed with very specific questions. Were there any textbooks at that time in the Bosniak language or the Bosnian language? I apologise. I have to interrupt you. Let us therefore focus, if we started talking about the school programmes and curricula in the former Yugoslavia, of course I understand your interest but we unfortunately do not have the time for that. So once again, were there any textbooks in general in the Bosniak language at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: I am profoundly convinced that Their Honours also understand these issues, of course, not to the same degree to which we understand it. In the school year 1991-92, no changes were made as far as the subject titled "Serbo-Croatian or Croato-Serbian language" were made in the -- and so -- and nothing was changed in the entire period of the development of the socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I have to interrupt you here because it seems to me that we now have the break and we will resume afterwards. We will continue exploring this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, before we have the witness here, I would like to say that Judge Clark won't be able to sit with us because of personal health, so in accordance with the Rule 15 bis (A), the remaining Judges of the Chamber decided to sit and continue to hear the case. It is so decided. Bring in the witness, please. Yes, Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we continue, I'd like to make an objection of some -- about something which was said prior to the break by Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. Krsnik and I'm referring to the transcript page 23, when Mr. Krsnik said the following, "Your Honours, we were tendered statements and testimonies made by an incompetent witness who was a mufti in Mostar and through this witness the learned friend made an attempt to paint a picture and now the Defence is trying to shed a few shreds of truth to that picture. Your Honours, I object to the -- I'm sorry, I went a bit fast. I object to the way Mr. Krsnik has characterised one of our Prosecution witnesses and I think witnesses for both parties should be treated with respect and that's my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is taken, and the -- but we believe that you have to make that objection right after his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes. My apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really do not know and see the exact point in the transcript of what I was in fact trying to say. I just said that we had witnesses that discussed this issue, linguistic and other issues, and now we have brought in a witness who is competent to speak about these issues, who is a meritorious witness, and this, Mr. Bos, was in fact the meaning of my words. I did not intend to describe it that way. I'm not going to comment on your witnesses. I will comment, if you will, your witnesses through my witnesses, and I will bring the competent people here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, your statement is in the record. You may proceed with this witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So Mr. Maric, we discussed the question before the break whether there were textbooks in the Bosnian language, whether there were these textbooks in the Bosnian curricula and programme and could you please be brief and focus? And I'm sure you can focus. You're a highly educated person and you will thus facilitate the work of both this Trial Chamber and the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll try to do my best but I have to share with you the facts that -- the facts. In school year 1992-93, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, we still used the same curriculum, the same programme and the same textbooks. So once again, the same school programme and the same textbooks, and these were the textbooks that were published by the Sujetlost and Veselin Maslesa publishing houses in Sarajevo. These textbooks were approved by the Ministry of Education of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As to the new school year, 1993-94, in fact -- I apologise. First 1992 and 1993, we initially started using these very same textbooks. Unfortunately, however, given the wartime situation in Sarajevo, new textbooks that were be used in the new school year could not be printed. Therefore, everybody concerned, from the territory of Posavina onward to Sarajevo and Herzegovina, had to do with what was available. In other words, we had to use the textbooks from the previous school year. However, since it regularly happens, as we all know, and we all went to school, that textbooks suffer from wear and tear. We were obliged to request assistance in terms of textbooks, supplies from Zagreb. Unfortunately in this very same school year, the publishing house called Skolska Knjiga of Zagreb only published those textbooks and in the number which they anticipated to be needed in the Republic of Croatia. So the school year in 1992-93, as far as textbooks are concerned, was a difficult year indeed. In the school year 1993-1994, given the fact that in Sarajevo that publishing and printing facilities were still not operating, and given the fact that not a single textbook could be published and printed there, we were compelled to once again ask the Ministry of Education of the Republic of Croatia to help us out. The ministry did help us, both for -- in terms of the students and pupils in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as helped tens of thousands of refugee students and pupils, refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina, who were present in the Republic of Croatia where they went to school, together with the local students and pupils, either thus going to the regular classes of the regular schools in the Republic of Croatia or to special newly-established and opened schools and thus both the Bosniaks and the Croats went to the same classes and to the same schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: With your permission, Mr. Maric, were there any separate curricula and programmes for Bosnians and were there ever any such things as Bosnian textbooks?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: This is what I was going to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you be perhaps more specific and more concise? I know that you have to explain these things but let us not do it at too great a length.

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Sir, Your Honours, it was only in school year 1994-95 that for the first time, it was outside our country that textbooks were published on the basis of the programmes and curricula adopted and approved by the central government in Sarajevo. So it was only in the school year 1994-95 that this happened. May I continue? In December of 1997, it was in Sarajevo that the ombudsman organised a round-table discussion devoted to the system of schools and education in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the course of the discussions of the round-table participants and the participants were former ministers of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina for education, then the ministers of cantons, furthermore, four professors from the United States of America. The data were tabled which of course I had been familiar with even before that, namely, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and now I'm only referring to that part that was usually referred to as Bosnian and Herzegovinian. We had no local textbooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to answer the following question. Did you too make changes in the curriculum and the programme? And were, in the first place, you at a position which allowed to you make these changes?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Somewhere at the beginning of my testimony, I stressed that using the existing curricula and school programmes, we tried only to eliminate from them only those elements which are alien to a democratic society, and in comparison with the curricula and school programmes that had been in use until the year 1992, through such a comparison one can easily see that no radical changes were made. Furthermore, in the course of the discussions held at the round table mentioned before, the ombudsman also submitted a report emphasising that these very same curricula and school programmes were also used in the territories of the Zupanijas or provinces with majority Croat population in the year 1997, and that there was no criticism voiced as far as their contents and substance are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, are you not familiar with the programme of the HDZ regarding the education and school programmes? Was their programme proposed by them any different? And do you know generally speaking what their position was?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: My apologies. Let me try to rephrase it. What was the HDZ programme as far as schools and education were concerned, if you're aware?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that. In our political declarations, there was always a chapter on education, culture, and science, and our position was always the same, that is that following the new democratic elections and changes, our education, our school system, should follow the best traditions of the free world and Europe. Of course, every school system is based on the national language and the national culture, and in multicultural communities, this aspect, this multiculturality is also taken into account. So on the basis of this political position, or these political principles, we reached two decrees in wartime circumstances of course, in 1993. One of them being a decree on elementary education --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honours. I think that my client is not feeling well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I just turned around and I realised that he's sick. May I go to my client, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course, of course. You may look into the matter and report to this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He can leave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I didn't have time to ask you whether he can be allowed to leave the courtroom. We can by all means proceed without his presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, the accused could be excused and be escorted out of the room and we will continue with the proceedings without his presence, with the agreement from the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my colleague has just told me that the security does not allow my client to have his nitroglycerine with him at all times. I should like to ask the permission for him to have his medication in case of emergency. I don't know what the situation is and what will happen. I hope that he will be examined today. As far as the health of my client is concerned, generally speaking, I do hope that the issue will be taken more seriously in the future. In the past seven or eight months, he has had only one medical examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, if your client needs a medical examination, we will entrust the Registrar to conduct it in due time, but we are not in the position to order your client to have certain medicines at hand. I think it is the job for the doctors, not for the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honour, but I think that he should be allowed to have them in the courtroom. It is the security that doesn't allow him to have his medication at all times, not the physicians, and a moment ago, he didn't have this medication with him. It was the guard who brought the medication and the doctor prescribed him this medication and recommended that he should have it with him at all times. It is a matter of security concerns. I think that he should be allowed to have his medication on him at all times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'll ask the Registrar to look into this matter. You may proceed, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Much obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, I think that we were discussing the school programme and curricula and the position of the HDZ regarding these issues. I'm sure you're more concentrated than I am. Would you please continue where you left off.

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: I was talking about the decrees governing the school system in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. We, and I am referring to the HZ HB government, adopted two such decrees. One was related to the elementary education and one to the secondary education in times of war, and in the presence of war danger. The decrees were published in the Official Gazette which is called Narodni List HZ HB, 293 and 1393, their respective numbers, that is. After the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was established in 1993, these decrees, with some minor amendments, became the law on elementary and secondary education. These two statutory texts regulated the school system and education in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. They were in existence until the Washington Accords, which stipulated that all existing arrangements should continue to apply until new relevant laws are passed by the constitutional assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the position as far as the language is concerned?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: In the socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, officially speaking, there were three languages, which were called the Macedonian language in Macedonia, the Slovenian language in Slovenia, and in the four remaining republics, that is the Republic of Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbia and Montenegro, the language was called differently. It actually consisted of -- the title consisted of two words; it was called Serbo-Croat or Croato-Serbian language. This phrase, which was actually the name of the official language, is indicative of its components. With the break-up of Yugoslavia, the language in the Republic of Croatia was renamed and became the Croatian language, the Croatian standard language. As for Bosnia and Herzegovina, every ethnic community in their relevant statutory text referred to the language which was spoken in Bosnia-Herzegovina and which differed slightly, not in any major way -- I want to make this point very clear -- as, in accordance with linguistic customs, normal linguistic customs, was referred to by using the name of the relevant ethnic community. Therefore, Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina called their language the Serbian language, the Croats referred to it as the Croatian language, whereas the Bosniaks, the group which at the time was still officially called Muslims, called their language the Bosnian language. It was only later on, a year or two later, that the language was called or became the Bosnian language. That was the situation, that was the reality in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the conflict, and it is the reality today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What language was spoken in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: As far as the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is concerned, but let me generally say that I believe that we all know that there is always a standard language, and the everyday language, which is characterised by numerous cultural, regional differences. Therefore, in HZ HB, the official language of the school system and the media, and for the purposes of public communication in general, was the Croatian standard language. However, we were very clear and explicit in saying that the area in question is also inhabited by other ethnic communities, the members of which, both in the official and everyday use of the language, were able or could refer to their language as the Bosnian language or the Serbian language, and use it accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, there is one thing I want to clarify at this point. There should be no mystery in these proceedings for all those activities going on. This Trial Chamber has made a decision to allow Mr. Naletilic to go back to the Detention Unit just now, just for the information of the Prosecution. I'm sorry for the interruption. Mr. Krsnik, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, very much, for this information. I'm sure that you could also see that I too was a bit impatient and confused as to what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, was it possible to learn the Bosniak language in schools and was there a department, an official linguistic department, for the Bosniak language? Were there any professors, any experts in the Bosniak language in the area at the time? I am referring to the year 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Speaking of 1992 and 1993, there were three departments, there were three chairs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, at the relevant universities or colleges, which taught the so-called Serbo-Croatian or Croato-Serbian language. During the war, Serbs in Croatia, at the teachers college, were referring to the language as the Serbian language. In Tuzla, Sarajevo and Mostar, for example, the language was officially called, as can be seen from students' official booklets, was described generally speaking in three ways, as the Bosnian language or the Serbo-Croatian or Croato-Serbian language or only as the Croatian language. One should note here that the structure of the language, the vocabulary and the syntax were in practical terms not changed in any way due to the change in the official name of the language. Up until then, the official language textbooks, the grammar books, at the time, both in schools and at the universities, were using the name Serbo-Croatian or Croato-Serbian language, depending on the origin of the author of the official grammar book in a given linguistic area, with the so-called linguistic variations or linguistic variants of the language. Here in The Hague, I had an opportunity to contact some people who studied the language here in Amsterdam, and I was able to see that they make a very clear distinction in these terms. This distinction is also made by this Tribunal because the documents that I have received are written in the so-called western variant of the language, if we are using the terms which were in use up until 1990 and which today, after the political changes, this variant of the language would be officially referred to as the Croatian standard language. It is probable -- actually I'm quite sure that the members of the Serb ethnic community, and this is something which I was able to observe from an interpreter here who is expressing herself in the Serbian language, I have seen that the practice of this Tribunal is such that it has accepted all three variants of the language, including the third one, which is today officially called the Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I merely wanted to ask you whether in 1991, 1992 and 1993, there were any professors of the Bosnian -- Bosniak language, and was this language being taught?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: In 1991 and 1992, there were no official grammar books of the Bosniak or the Bosnian language. Of course, there was a whole range of scientific texts written on the issue, including the book written by Professor Dzevad Bihac [phoen] who is a professor at the University of Sarajevo. He published a book entitled, "The Language of Bosnian Muslims." He, as a linguistic authority amongst the Bosniak population, as early as 1991, he still did not refer to the language as the Bosnian or the Bosniak language. I don't know exactly when it was that the decision was made within the Bosniak component, that the official use of the title, that is that the official title would be the Bosniak or the Bosniak language. I don't know when that happened. As for the possibilities of teaching this language, be it the Croatian, the Serbian or the Bosniak language, all of us who have a degree in Slavic studies, including my colleagues which I had an opportunity to meet here in Amsterdam, know perfectly well that they are competent enough to teach the language which used to be called the Serbo-Croatian language or the Croato-Serbian language and which today is officially called either the Bosnian, the Croatian or the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, let me show you a document at this point, ID D1/95, 96 and 97.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have all these three documents, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the interpreters, my colleague, Mr. Pinter, provided the relevant documents yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: We were just wondering if there is an English translation of these documents, and if not, we object.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that Mr. Bos knows perfectly well that we do not have translation of this -- these documents. Mr. Bos, I think I informed you of this fact yesterday. I don't know why you are asking the question now. That is exactly the reason why we provided the interpretation booths with the -- with these originals and I think I already told you that we didn't have the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you understand that this Trial Chamber is seized with a motion filed by the Prosecution, objecting to the proceedings without the translation, and we have already entrusted the Registrar to look into this matter. I hope this matter will be solved next week. With this understanding -- with this understanding, shall we proceed without translation for a while, since those documents are very simple documents, we could know the contents through the oral interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. These are very simple documents indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we object for the record, and it may be if there is more documents which are not in the English version, we may need more time for cross-examination, so -- but I'm in your hands if you need to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, my suggestion is that we proceed based on those documents, with the understanding that this translation will be supplied as soon as possible. Yes, Mr. Krsnik, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is not the time for me to say that at this point in time, but let me tell you that some of the documents we tendered in for translation were not translated so far, and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. some are still being translated, but we didn't want to interrupt, to halt, to slow down the proceedings. I just want to mention it for the record. It is not for the first time that we have entered the situation. It is not for the first time that we have shared this concern of ours with the Trial Chambers but the learned friend got the documents, they know what the documents are, they have their own translation service. This is just a tactic. I will not go on, Your Honours. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise to Mr. Krsnik. The last statement, Mr. President, is untrue. Speaking on behalf of the Prosecution, the Office of the Prosecutor, we share with the Defence the same translation unit. It's the translation unit for this Tribunal. We all share the same people. We all receive translations from the same people, under the same conditions, and under the same time constraints. We are not in a better position than the Defence in respect of translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I got some letters from the Registrar. He promised me that he will put the translation for this case as the priority in the translation. They promise to do the translation and supply it to us as soon as possible. In the meantime, we will make decisions on the motions filed by the Prosecution. Mr. Krsnik, shall we drop this issue and proceed with the direct examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at this document and tell us, one after the other, what you can see from these documents?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Can I start?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, could you please put on the first document, namely, on the ELMO, ID D -- D1/95?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You can watch it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Very well. Can I start? What I see in front of me is a report card on the completion of the first grade of grammar school in Zenica in school year 1992-93.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us where is Zenica located, under whose authority it is?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Zenica is a town in central Bosnia, northwest of Sarajevo, some 50 kilometres distance to Sarajevo. At this point in time, when this report card was issued, it was under the authority of the BIH army. First let me tell you something about the form itself of this school report. This form continues the practice of similar forms that were issued and used by schools until the outbreak of the war in 1991-92. I am, however, surprised to see that this is called Uvjerenje, which is a certificate, although usually students, at the end of the school year, would receive what is called Svjedodzba or Svjedocanstvo, a report. Svjedocanstvo, the latter term, was the Bosniak term used. Secondly, the only change or novelty I can see here is the following. The box which is entitled "subjects taught", nastavni predmeti, were in the past, the first item usually was Serbo-Croatian or Croato-Serbian. This item is empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you show us where specifically you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: It is empty, it's just a dotted line, and it is here inserted "mother" maternji, mother tongue. Officially, no ministry at all used this category, "mother tongue." Neither in the period of the socialist regime nor in the course of the war. Secondly, what I can also note here is the following. The language in which this report or this certificate, in terms of its form, is concerned, i.e., the printed part of the text and not the part which is written by hand, simply continues the practice of the two variants, the two language variants used, which can very easily be seen, for example, if we go down here to the subject concerning history, historija, then the next one, geography, geografija zemejopis, and the same applies to chemistry, although the two linguistic alternatives have not been used consistently through this document. For example, if consistency were to be observed, instead of fizicko vaspitanje, which is physical education, the wording should also be fizicko odgoj. And then in some other parts, this two-language pattern was not used. For example, where it says opstina, municipality, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, we usually used opcina, opstina, both forms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, this is very difficult to interpret because unfortunately or fortunately in English, there is only one word for all these two linguistic alternatives. So to expedite the matters, I'd like you to tell us, are you familiar with the ethnic background, ethnicity of the person who graduated from this first grade?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Obviously, on the basis of this document, because it is not said anything as to that matter, apart from the citizenship, I cannot say anything as to what is the ethnicity of this individual student.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, this was the year 1992-93. Can you tell us whether the person concerned is a Muslim, a Croat, a Serb?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Judging by the first name, the family name, and the father's name, I can say that this is a student, a female student to be more specific, who most probably is of Croat origin but of course, that is something for her to decide personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Let me add something else and draw your attention to another fact. Have a look at the top. It says, "The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina" at the very beginning of this document. So if we were to follow the same analogy in terms of the name of the state or country concerned, the same should be repeated in the seal, the seal, the state seal, through which the state had authorised this document. However, down here, it says, "The Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina" in the seal. In other words, one cannot, on the basis of this document, know what state is referred to. One name is used at the top, and another within the seal. I should also like to draw your attention to this seal here which is the seal of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which on the basis of the democratic elections was changed, or avoided if anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you proceed to the next document, ID D1/96?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: This is the same female student that we had before. Now we are in the next school year, 1993-94, second grade of this secondary school. Now I can see that we have two coats of arms, one which is an integral part of the form itself, which is this coat of arms on top of the name [B/C/S spoken], certificate, and this very same coat of arms is repeated in the seal, which, as far as I can see it from this document, says, "The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina" in Cyrillic and in Latin script, the grammar school in Zenica. Furthermore, what is new in this form is that there is no category called "mother tongue" anymore. This tongue in this document is called the Bosnian language. We still have this dual linguistic dual use of certain subjects which was a characteristic feature of the eastern and western linguistic models, that is historija povijest for history, geografija zemljopis is for geography, and we can also note that here, the subjects' titles were changed. For example, now we have a subject called [indiscernible], which used -- which would be translated into English, physical and health education. It used to be vaspitanje, and now we have the same term, which is used both by the Bosniaks and the Croats, which is odgoj in English, education.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could we proceed? Let us have document ID D1/97. Did you say that this was the same female student?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can see, it's the same school, the grammar school of Zenica, school year 1994-95. This student seemed to have performed very well. Now, as far as the form itself is concerned, it remains unchanged compared to the one before, but I see that in the list of subjects, we have a different reference to the mother tongue. In school year 1994-95, when the clashes ceased, when the Washington constitution had been passed, it was now also recognised, namely the fact was recognised that in Bosnia, the official languages were Serbian, Croat and Bosnian, and this student, probably her headmaster identified her as of Croatian background, has, under the mother tongue, Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, are you familiar with any protests lodged by Croats or other individuals of ethnic -- of different ethnic background as to the fact that they are not learning Bosniak language?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Yes, of course, there were such protests or reactions. We heard about them. And they were manifested in terms of silent protests because at wartime, in a wartime situation, it's not always good to voice your concerns aloud particularly if you're a student or a parent of a student.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I will now show you the document, P168.1, and I will tell you that it was said in this courthouse that this very document is a proof of the fact that HDZHB was imposing the Croatian language and that the government HDZHB was thus trying to show that the Bosniaks were prevented from using their mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Can I continue? Well, here, I can see certificate on top, we have the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna. If you compare these two forms, in terms of the printed text, you can see that there was one single choice, those certificates which were uniform throughout the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina in school year 1990-1991. However, since, as it says, the date at which it was issued was the 18th of August, 1992, since at that time, in Sarajevo, no certificates were printed or at least we didn't have any access to them, therefore I, as the head of this department, decided to have these forms printed and to follow the earlier form and pattern of these certificates. The only thing we did do is the following: Upon the decision of the government of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, we added in the certificate the national, Croatian coat of arms which was usually and generally used in this type of documents before, in the period until 1990, the coat of arms of the republics were used and since the coat of arms of Bosnia-Herzegovina was a socialist coat of arm without any national elements in it and it was not accepted by any of the three peoples which one could see from the earlier documents. We saw that the Bosniaks decided to use the new coat of arms with the fleur-de-lis, the Serbs used the coat of arms with the eagles and the Croats, following their historic traditions, decided to use the Croatian historical coat of arms. Here in the list of subjects, the Croatian standard language was used but you will note that this language is indeed very understandable to each student coming from all three ethnic backgrounds in Bosnia-Herzegovina and just like the female student in Zenica, had no problems to understand when it said here, under "mother tongue," Bosnian, it was not a problem for the pupils and students in this part of Bosnia-Herzegovina to accept this terminology, particularly since the terminology used was the terminology which was used by the teachers, and no teacher changed these certificates in any radical way. The teachers were not offering new terminology, new grammar rules, et cetera.
