It was only in political terms that after the democratic elections, it was established that in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in a country of three peoples, and in conformity with the traditions of democratic society, every people is -- each people are allowed to use their own language.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were you using the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. You see, I myself have made the life of interpreters more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you then please tell us if somebody insisted, could the word "Bosniak language" be used under the subject "mother tongue"?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Certainly. Meetings of headmasters of both elementary and secondary schools that were held regularly. To be able to tackle the daily issues that cropped up in our schools, there were statements made by the headmasters that in practice, apart from the subject "mother tongue", practically nothing was changed, and it was particularly emphasised that no professor, no teacher, is allowed to coerce or influence students and pupils, bring them into an unpleasant position because of the fact that perhaps they do not always know each of the double alternatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. Now, I'm a bit confused. You say that the Bosniak language is not being allowed, and in 1991, 1992, 1993, in fact there was no Bosniak language, was there?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Of course not. It is -- you cannot find it in any official document. The government of Bosnia and Herzegovina had not adopted any new grammar or other rules, but of course the political parties that were established in Bosnia and Herzegovina used in both written and spoken language, which was different because of the new democratic changes. It was the language which they, as individuals, referred to as Bosniak, as Serbian, as Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well. I will now share with you a statement repeatedly made here in this courtroom. It was said that teachers and professors on a systematic basis were expelling -- so were teachers and professors systematically persecuted, fired, expelled from schools if they were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: All our documents, I'm referring to the documents of the Ministry of Education of the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna and later on of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, indicate that all teachers and professors remain on their jobs and there is no single act or regulation issued by the ministry demanding from the headmasters to fire anyone from their job on grounds of their ethnic -- their ethnicity. But what was going on in those territories where war was raging, where clashes took place, whether at the local levels there were certain difficulties and problems, well, of course, they did crop up because it was not just schools but entire towns, or entire parts of the population that were abandoning certain territories because of war conflicts. Among those who were leaving their territories for one reason or another, which all had to do with wartime situation, a certain number were also teachers and professors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. I'll show you document ID D1/98, and will ask you to tell this Court what this is all about. Witness, could you please give the usher the book you have in your hand and tell us whether this document makes part of this book and what the book is all about?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Well, this is a collection of publications and articles on the elementary and secondary schools in Mostar during the war. It was published by the social affairs department office in Mostar. This collection is not an official document issued by the ministry, but rather published by the social affairs service of Mostar, and it was published in June, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you tell us what does this collection tell us, cover?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, this collection consists of publications and articles by different authors who come from the town of Mostar, most of them are professors or teachers who here describe the organisation of the school system in the school year 1992-93.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Does it also discuss the general personnel issues, in terms of the teaching staff in -- under wartime circumstances?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Here in front of us we have an article of this sort, which describes the teaching staff personnel issues and wartime circumstances, using, for the sake of illustration, the example of the secondary construction engineering school in Mostar. One can very easily see here that in school year 1992-93, classes were organised and held, and here we have a list of those teachers and professors who were full time employees of this school. We have in total 27 professors and then in the next section, the author says that the professors, under numbers 1 to 9 above, abandoned their jobs prior to the open aggression on Mostar and this happened in the so-called war between the JNA or Serbian war, waged against the Bosniaks and Croats. These individuals, therefore, listed under 1 to 9, as far as we can tell by their names and surnames, can be identified as members of the Serbian people. So it was before the attack of the JNA and the so-called reservists. It seems that these teachers, these professors, had known about the upcoming attacks. They left their jobs and only Muslims and Croats remained in the school. But as far as I can tell, some Serbs as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. Can you tell us whether these teachers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, you spent a lot of time on the issue of education which did not appear in your 65 ter filings. I hope you could get over this section as soon as possible so that we could hear more about the other two issues, that is his life in Mostar during the war in 1992 and 1993, as well as about exchanging of detainees between the parties to the conflict. We will resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, how long are you going to take in your direct examination?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. Another 30 minutes. But my witness is very talkative and his answers are rather long, but I do hope to be able to finish within half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: According to your filings, it's about 90 minutes for the direct examination. I have to remind you about that. Bring the witness, please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, we will have to proceed faster. I will try to phrase my questions with that in view. Were Bosniaks, according to this text, ever sacked and expelled from work, or did they retain their employment throughout 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Most of them held their employment, whether some of them left or not, I don't really know. This was not part of my competences but I know that no official school body ever requested any teacher or professor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. Krsnik, I hope that the witness did not interpret Mr. Krsnik's warning that he should speed up in his speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, you have heard Her Honour Judge Diarra. Do not speak faster but let us try to shorten the answers and make them more concise. Witness, was anyone expelled on account of Bosniak ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: No, no one. This was never said publicly by any member of the ministry, nor was it done in any official manner through any statutory provision or other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Who was the director of the grammar school in Mostar? Did these people continue working throughout this period of time?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: I cannot know in precise terms what the personnel issues were in detail in 1992 and 1993 and 1993-1994. However, what I do know is that the schoolmasters of elementary and secondary schools were mostly people, who throughout 1990 and 1991, had held the same post, that is who had already been schoolmasters, Croats and Bosniaks alike. Specifically I know that the head of the Mostar grammar school remained on his post throughout the war, including the Croatian and Bosniak conflict, and he was a Muslim or a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What was the situation at the university? Was there any discrimination there?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: As for the University of Mostar, throughout this period of time, that is the school year 1992-93, as can be seen from the list of employees, and I am referring to the professors at the university and at the local colleges, over 35 of them. As far as I know, and in view of the information I had, were Bosniaks. There was a small number of Serbs as well. As for the school year of 1993 and 1994, in the midst of the conflict in Mostar, both Croats and Muslims fled on account of the hostilities. Therefore, in that school year, the number of both of them decreased. However, over 20 or 25 Bosniaks were still working at the universities as full-time professors or teaching assistants. Some of them were members of the board of the university, such as Mr. Dedic. I think that at the beginning of the school year, the dean of the construction -- of the civil engineering department was also -- was Mr. Behmen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: A Bosniak as well?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot recall all of them, all of the professors who taught at the Mostar university at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was the University of Mostar or parts thereof ever relocated during that period of time? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately on two occasions, first during the attack by the JNA, the faculty was forced to discontinue their classes, as was the case with teachers in elementary and secondary schools, and proceed with their examinations outside Mostar. Unfortunately, the same situation reoccurred during the conflict between Bosniaks and Croats, when the conflict was raging in the town itself. In order not to lose that school year, the head of the university, the dean, decided to relocate certain departments of the University of Mostar and organised classes in the town of Neum, where, thanks to numerous hotel facilities, it was possible to organise instruction. Part of instruction was going on in Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Including Bosniaks, that is Bosniak professors who also continued to teach?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Yes, of course, those who remained continued with their work. I did not follow directly their attendance and their work but they proceeded with the normal work, to the extent it was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did Bosniak professors during the conflict between Bosniaks and Croats also teach in Neum and Siroki Brijeg, that is where the faculty was relocated?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Yes, and after we returned to Mostar, they continued with their teaching.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Once again, my apologies to the Court. It was me who sped up this time. Judge Diarra, I believe my remark was accurately entered into the record. Let us move on. Would you be so kind to tell us something about your membership in the commission for exchange of war prisoners? Could you tell us when that was and what your duties included?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: After the breakout of the conflict in April, 1992, and the fighting which took place in the area of Kupres, both sides, that is the JNA, the Serb side, and the then Bosniak and Croat side in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were prisoners of war, that is both sides detained a certain number of prisoners of war. At the beginning of the conflict, as early as April, 1992, only a week into the conflict, after the fighting in Kupres calmed down a little bit, we started negotiations on the exchange of POWs. Initially I was a member of this commission and I subsequently became its head. The negotiations were conducted under the auspices of the European observers and the Red Cross. Between April, 1992 and sometime in autumn, 1992, during that period of time, we held talks almost twice a week in the villages of Zitnic and Pakovo Selo. At the separation line with the UNPA, UN protected areas, we were also accompanied by Mr. Dieter Wolfmann who is the deputy high representative in Sarajevo today and later on, with Mr. Castella. Each meeting was attended of course by the representatives of the International Red Cross and we were very fast in agreeing on the exchanges of POWs on both sides. However, a smaller -- small part of those POWs spent quite some time in detention. They were the subject of our talks for a long time, and then due to some practical reasons, the negotiations were relocated to the separation line in Bosnia and Herzegovina, to the area of Livansko Polje, the area of the town of Livno, in particular, in the towns of Kovacic and Celibici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I don't think we need to go into such details. My question was whether you were the president of the commission who took equal care of the exchange of Bosniak and Croat POWs.

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Yes. Of course. Because the JNA, who was party to those negotiations at that time, held mostly Croat and Muslim prisoners. However, there were individual members of other ethnic groups. As you probably know, the town of Kupres counted all three ethnic communities as their inhabitants, and all three were captured and detained alike. So with no -- we spoke about prisoners of war, not about members of such and such ethnic community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. When did your mandate in the commission cease?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: I negotiated with the Serb side, as we used to call them, until the autumn of 1993, until most of the POWs on both sides, in the southern part, were released, and when unfortunately, the conflict opposing Bosniaks and Croats started. I stopped conducting these negotiations but I continued negotiating -- I'm sorry, but my deputy, Mr. Zeljko Radic and Mr. Berislav Busic continued with these negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We are moving towards the end of the examination. I have only two or three questions left for you. Before I show you some documents, let me ask you whether you personally know, Seid Smajkic, the mufti?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did he ever tell you any of his objections as to the discrimination going on?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Mr. Mukic and myself, together with another multi-national delegation participated in January 1993 in the prayers which were organised in Asisi, together with Cardinal Puljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Excuse me, what country?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: In Italy. So together with Cardinal Puljic, Mr. Mandelbaum who was a member of the Jewish community in Mostar, the prayers were also attended by a representative of the Islamic religious community, including Mr. Smajkic. We travelled together. From Mostar we travelled by bus to Split, where we took a plane to Italy, to Rome. We stayed there for a week. We were accommodated in the same hotel. We used the same means of transport to reach Asisi and we participated in the same congregation which conducted these prayers. We returned together. I got off at Grude, some 40 kilometres before Mostar, and I parted in a very friendly manner with Mr. Smajkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did he have any objections that I mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Unfortunately, this was the last time that we met. I haven't spoken to him since but as far as that period of time is concerned, he voiced no such objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I can tell you this because he was a public witness. He was the one who showed us the school report which I produced, and he testified about discrimination against Muslims who were allegedly expelled from schools, solely on account of their ethnicity. He also testified that no other language but the Croatian language was allowed in schools. How do you respond to that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: During the five days that we spent travelling together, me and Mr. Smajkic talked, we spent several hours talking, and I did not notice that he didn't understand me. I could perfectly understand him, and as far as I am concerned, I didn't in any way alternate the way I speak. And I know our teachers didn't do it either, that there were no changes in the way they spoke. I don't know what kind of educational background Mr. Smajkic has in terms of linguistics but I do believe that as far as the issues of the language are concerned, he is not quite an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Sir, the people who lived in HZ HB, were they able to choose religious instruction according to their wishes?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning, when we started with the religious instruction, my ministry drafted a questionnaire --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, let me ask the assistance of the usher. Is this the questionnaire you're talking about? I believe we provided the Prosecution with the questionnaire in question but my colleague is telling me she is not so sure about that. You'll be able to check. It will be on the ELMO in a moment. If you have not received it I will withdraw it of course and I will rely solely on the witness. Do you have the questionnaire in -- that we are talking about, Mr. Prosecutor? It bears number ID D1/99.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, sorry, we don't have that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll withdraw the document and the witness will simply provide us with an oral explanation of the issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: In accordance with the practice of the religious instruction in school, in general terms, as it is in certain countries in Europe, we did not impose the subject but we made it an optional subject in schools. So it was not obligatory for the student to take up religious instruction. So in order to find out who wishes to study -- to have religious instruction as a school subject, and which religious instruction in particular, we drafted a questionnaire which is of course no invention of ours. I presume that this is how it is done in other places as well. So as far as the students of elementary schools are concerned, we asked the parents of those students to state whether they want their children to have religious instruction in school. We also asked them to sign the questionnaire and also to circle the kind of religious instruction they wanted to choose. The Orthodox one, the Islamic one, or the Catholic one, or the Jewish one. So it was only after the parents of the elementary school students made it clear and expressed their wish, did we organise, on the basis of this information, or enable the religious instruction in elementary school. As for secondary schools, it was the students who expressed their wishes in this questionnaire because we believe them to be more mature enough to take that decision. One more thing, those who choose on an optional basis to attend religious instruction, were then, of course, obliged to continue with the practice throughout the school year. Of course, it is possible for them to give it up at one point in time but this was specifically stated in the papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We have to hurry up a little bit, Mr. Maric. Let me show you now three documents: 102, 103, and 104, that is ID D1/102, 3, and 4. This is my penultimate question and then we will finally have the ultimate question. Witness, would you please have a look at this document and tell us what it purports to be? But try to be as brief as possible because we have to wind up.

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: I'm afraid I will to have read this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Well, I will need some time to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Please, take your time but try to read as fast as you can. Tell us briefly about the contents of this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: First of all, in the preamble of the document, that is in the heading of the document I can see "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What document are you reading, please?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: 102, D1/102, so in the heading of the document, I can see, "Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the command of the 4th Corps." The addressee is the headquarters of the supreme command and in the brackets for the Ministry of Education, Culture, and Sports. The contents of the document pertain to the school system, hence I'm somewhat surprised that the command of the 4th Corps with Mr. Arif Pasalic as the signatory of the document who I know completed a military academy and does not have an educational background, should write to an institution which, as far as I know, did not exist. The staff of the supreme command -- I don't know whether there was a Ministry of Education, Culture, and Sports, which would have been linked to the supreme command or it may have been subordinated to the supreme command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Boss?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I don't think that the witness should speculate on what Mr. Pasalic could do on the basis of this document. He doesn't have knowledge on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very sorry, Your Honours, that we do not have the translation of the document, which was signed by Mr. Arif Pasalic, the document in which he discusses the educational issues. That is what is contained in the document. It was not the speculation on the part of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, since we don't have the translation at our hands, you may ask several questions to lay the foundation of this document first, then proceed with your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Would you please tell us the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: 31st March, 1993. Only several days after my return from Rome with Mr. Smajkic did the outbreak between the Muslims and Croats in Mostar start.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Does this constitute direct interference and influence in the army, that is the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in matters pertaining to education and is this an imposition of school programmes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I object to the leading nature of this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik. Rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you explain for us, then, the contents of this document, briefly, please? We are really pressed with time.

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: What surprises me here in this document is the fact that the command of the 4th Corps of the BH Army, which does not have education within its competences, should order to the Minister of Education what they should do, that they should report to them what was going on in Mostar. At least, that's what is written in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well. Can we have document 103 and 104 at the same time? Would you please read both of them and make a joint comment on these two documents? I believe that once we've heard the -- once we receive the translation, the documents will speak for themselves. Did you read both documents through?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: No. This is a lengthy document indeed, and, you know, there is a certain speed of reading which I cannot go beyond. From the part that I was able to read, I could see that here, schools and school systems are discussed by somebody who is not an expert in this area, how it functions, et cetera, because once again, it is Mr. Arif Pasalic, the commander of the 4th Corps that signed the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Are you referring to document ID D1/103?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What is the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: 19th May [sic], 1993. In this document, the author entertains a variety of statements that are not true, so in fact, I would have to go through the document, sentence by sentence, to show to you that the facts are not true. The second document I have to go on reading, the second document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We have a correction to make in the transcript. The witness said 19th of March, 1993 and not May. Would you please correct this? The date of the document is 19th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: This second document is in fact a continuation of the former.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: This is document ID D1/104, date?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: March 23, 1993. Now, the same author, the commander of the 4th Corps, signed as commander Mr. Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What does it say here?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: It says the army of BIH, commander of the 4th Corps. Here he is trying to describe the situation in -- at the university, which he is evidently not familiar with. He describes the confiscation of the university's property, who confiscated this, if we know that the buildings, what was left after the Serb destruction was still there with the same chancellor, with the same deans. Let me remind you that the conflict between Bosniaks and Croats had not started yet on the 23rd of March, 1993 in Mostar. What, however, I'm particularly surprised by, in fact I'm not surprised by it because this really happened, because Mr. Arif Pasalic in fact was the very person that tried to be the master of the war there. In the last paragraph he says, I quote, "Not -- well quite a few teachers are getting ready to reject further work in -- at the university. It is very probable they will do it in an organised manner." I wonder where the commander of the 4th Corps learned about the plans and intentions of the university professors of Bosniak nationality. Now, this date is the 23rd of March, 1993. Unfortunately, however, this turned out to be true. It was then later on that it was demanded from the university professors to withdraw from their posts at the university. This happened later on, with the elementary school teachers, the secondary school professors, but at the university level, the other professors remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, let us proceed to the last document, Prosecution document P102 -- sorry, of the date of the document is November 12, 1991. Prosecution document IC/2 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: It's IAC/2. The record reflects IC/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could the English version be put on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do we have it? I have it. I will give it to you. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell us whether this is you? Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this document. I note that it does not feature my signature. Now, why am I saying that this is not an authentic document? With your permission, have a look at the preamble, where it says, "The Croatian Democratic Union, the Travnik regional union," et cetera, "the Herzegovina regional community, the Travnik regional community." And then later on, Regional Crisis Staff for the Travnik regional community is referred to. Had this been an authentic document, had this been a document that I could sign, then I certainly would have paid enough attention to the fact that in administrative and legal terms, it be drafted correctly. This is one thing to say. Secondly, in this period, in November, 1991, I was the President of the HVO, under my leadership of the civilian HVO -- no, actually this is the year 1991. This is not the HVO. So I am the President of the municipality in Grude and I have about 100 employees in my administration, of which some ten were lawyers, and their job description included the request that they keep minutes, to be those who will keep minutes, and this can very clearly be seen from the documents. As to the text, I did not analyse it in great detail but I cannot recognise this document as my document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: If by any coincidence you were the person who kept the minutes, would you have signed it?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: I probably would have signed it. As far as I can recall, from my entry into the municipal administration, I was not the person who would keep the records. There were people either at the municipal level or the ministry level, when I had people who were knowledgeable in administration matters, and they were those who made sure that this type of illiterate document be drafted in an administrative and correspondence-related matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Another question. Mr. Maric, on the 17th of September, 1992, did you visit Dr. Franjo Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: On the 17th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: I went to visit President Tudjman with certain delegations but whether on that very same date I visited him as well, I would have to -- my memory would have to be refreshed through a document. At this point in time, I couldn't tell you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I will now show you the document PT number 5. PT 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I have also the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you get the Croatian version?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did I show you this document before?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: This is a transcript?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: I did not see it. May I be allowed some time to go through the first few pages so as to refresh my memory?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of the first few pages, judging by the names mentioned here, Mr. Brkic and some others whom I can recognise, and I'm just going through the names of those who spoke, I also attended one meeting where some of these people were also present. It might have been September 17, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you take page P5L, P/5L.

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Here we can see your name -- family name. My first question, would you read this through and tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could we have the English version on the ELMO so that we Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. can follow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think Mr. Usher is trying to find the right page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I will tell you in the English version, it's page -- [Interpretation] Unfortunately, Your Honours, unfortunately, this text was not translated into English in its entirety. I have just been warned about that fact by my colleague. Your Honours, the entire translation of the transcript into English was not brought in, only parts of the translation were brought in. This page is page 9 in the English transcript. It's a very short page. Your Honours, let me just tell you this. In the English language, you see this very short paragraph, while in the Croatian language, we have three pages and a half of this text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that there are some experts on translation in this Tribunal. They could verify the corresponding pages of this translation. You may proceed with your question, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you read it?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Can I have a few more moments?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can we proceed?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Just two more sentences, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: My first question, Mr. Maric. Did anybody tell you at any moment in time that the discussion was taped?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you or anyone else ever get a copy of it?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: No, I didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Is what is written here true?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: I read it very quickly and on the basis of what I have testified in this courtroom and upon a subtle analysis, one could see that this is not my style. Therefore, I cannot sign it, endorse it, as an authentic style of mine. It's a transcript, it's a recording which reflects my opinions but I would never be able to authorise them as mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. Thank you, Your Honours. This was my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you took about 190 minutes in your direct examination. You promised us to finish your direct examination in 90 minutes. The time you used doubled. I think this Trial Chamber has the right to stop you, or cut you short, for the following witnesses in the future. Yes, Mr. Bos, your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I may just organise myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have a set of exhibits which we would like to use in the cross-examination of this witness and can hand over the copies of those exhibits right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: There is one exhibit which is not in this binder, and that's the exhibit I'd like to start off with, and I have it here. It's a map of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you going to furnish us with this map? All we have -- or we already have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, I have one map which is in colour and I have black and white copies. I could furnish the black and white copies. And perhaps we could put the colour copy on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please. Well, Mr. Bos, does this map have a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I believe that this would be then Exhibit P906, if I'm not mistaken. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please. Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who prepared this map? Who is the author of this map and on what basis and grounds was it drafted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, this map only serves as a kind of indicative purpose to facilitate the proceedings. It's not very important unless later on you found it very essential to your case. You may raise this issue. Mr. Bos, you may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the origin of the map can be found in the right corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Diarra.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Diarra, that's correct. Indeed, and in fact, it's a map which is produced by the Office of the Prosecutor from our mapping department.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, good afternoon. My name is Roland Bos from the Office of the Prosecutor and I'm going to ask you some questions in cross-examination. I'd like to start off with this map and I think you have already had a chance to familiarise yourself. Is it correct, Mr. Maric, that this is a map of Bosnia-Herzegovina and -- with the municipalities of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that the municipalities indicated in the orange-red colour are in fact the municipalities that were included in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, on the basis of the establishment of Herceg-Bosna on 18 November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: And what are your specific questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, I'll get to that. You've stated in your examination-in-chief that all the municipalities of Herceg-Bosna comprised of a majority of Croats; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: I do not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Is it true that the municipalities in Herceg-Bosna -- isn't it true that you said that they were comprised of all the municipalities in which the population on the basis of the 1991 census, comprised -- that the municipalities comprised -- that each municipality of the Herceg-Bosna had a majority of Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: I can here see a map, the external boundaries of which are the recognised boundaries of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Furthermore, I can see the section whose author I do not, which is in a different colour, and I know that these municipalities here were, but not in their totality at the meeting held on November 18, 1991, were merged into the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes. And isn't it true that in your statements, you said that all these municipalities, which are indicated here as the territory of the -- of the Community of Herceg-Bosna, that for each municipality, the majority -- that the Croatian population in each of the municipalities had a majority in that municipality? That's what you stated in your examination-in-chief. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: I would like us to go back. This is not true, because I am very well familiar with the general structure of the population of these municipalities. Kotor Varos, for example, and Kakanj, for these two municipalities I know for sure that the Croatian population was not a majority. And the same applies to the municipality of Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But in your examination-in-chief, you stated that all the municipalities of Herceg-Bosna all had a majority of Croats. That's what you stated in your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Over the last two, three hours, I know more or less what I said, but I was certainly -- I didn't put it that way, or maybe it was not interpreted properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, isn't it true that Herceg-Bosna consisted of 28 municipalities?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: I wouldn't know it, the number of the municipalities off the cuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: All right. Well, what would you say to this statement, that if I say that the Herceg-Bosna had 28 municipalities and of those 28 municipalities, there were only 12 municipalities where the Croatian population had an absolute majority, meaning that more than 50 per cent of the population was Croat? Four of those 28 municipalities, there was a relative majority of the Croats, meaning there was -- the majority was Croat but not an absolute majority. And 12 of these municipalities, there wasn't neither an absolute majority or a relative majority of Croatian population. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Well, I know that in the municipality of Jablanica, which had 12.000 inhabitants, there were 2.000 or so Croats. The Skender Vakuf municipality had, I think, 25 inhabitants and 4.000 to 5 and a half thousand Croats. All these municipalities can be discussed and compared in these terms, the municipalities you're asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: The statement I just put to you, would you agree with this, that on the basis of the 1991 census, that there were, as I just said, only 12 municipalities with an absolute majority and four with a relative majority of Croatian people and 12 where there wasn't any majority? Would you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: I would have to look at the statistical data once again. I'm not an expert in statistics and I'm not a lawyer either. You could see from my previous testimony that I was involved in linguistic and educational matters in general. These are the issues that I don't feel competent enough to talk about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, you testified on three exhibits of the Defence which were Exhibits D1/95, 96, and 97, which -- if those documents could be placed in front of the witness again. Now, Witness, I don't have an English translation of this document so it's a bit difficult for me to work with this, but you explained this document -- let me first ask you. Was this the first time that you saw this document, when it was shown to you in court? Did you have any prior knowledge of this document?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Yes, because within my ministry, the regional or Zupanija ministry, I have a whole range of documents which were brought by the students who had in the meantime changed schools, and all of them who had come either from Republika Srpska or some Bosniak schools, had to bring with them all the documents when moving to a new school and these old documents as it is customary are then examined and then stored in the files, and if necessary, the appropriate inspection is done and again if necessary, the documents are being approved as acceptable. That is, the document is valid enough and meets the relevant criteria as they are in accordance with the school programme. There weren't such documents from the area of Republika Srpska or the area which -- areas which were under the Bosniak control -- excuse me. There are such documents coming from both areas. And regardless of whether they are from elementary schools or secondary schools, they were -- they had to be approved as valid for us, and that was the case with these documents here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you, Witness, because the point I want to make is if we look at -- well, any document. Let's put the first one. I don't know if you have D1/95 in front of you. Which municipality is mentioned on this document?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: No mention is made of the municipality of the school in question. The town of Zenica is mentioned here. I don't know whether it comprises one or more municipalities, so that goes -- this is as far as Zenica is concerned. We have the place of birth of the student, as far as I can see, and also -- yes, only the place of birth, which is the municipality of Zenica. So I'm making a different distinction here between --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Would you agree that this is probably a document which comes from a school in the municipality of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That is obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: That's the only thing I wanted to know. My next question is: Did the municipality of Zenica, did that fall within the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: That's all I wanted to know. Thank you. Now, would be -- I'd like to ask you some questions about your political views, and first of all, do you remember -- and I'm going back now to the 2nd of February, 1992. Do you remember that a meeting was held by the Croatian Democratic Community in Siroki Brijeg? And this is the period just before the referendum. Do you recall that meeting? And the meeting was discussing the Croatian position on the referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Maybe to refresh your memory a bit more, the meeting was chaired by Mr. Stjepan Kljujic, who was then the President of the HDZ, and it was also attended by a high-ranking delegation from the Republic of Croatia headed by Stjepan Mesic. Do you recall that meeting and were you present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: I did attend that meeting. I remember this meeting, not in detail, though, because it was a long time ago, but generally speaking, I know about this meeting and I remember attending it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you recall what was your political opinion on the functioning of Mr. Kljujic as president of the HDZ at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kljujic and myself had opposing political views on certain issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you be a -- elaborate a bit on that? What was the difference in opinion?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: I think that the basis of our political differences can be summed as follows: Mr. Kljujic, for reasons unknown to me, changed his political views from the time he became the President of the HDZ until this date, and his views and positions were not consistent with the political programme and platform of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, although he was the leader of the party. What I didn't accept, and what I objected to politically speaking was the fact that we could not accept an unitary Bosnia and Herzegovina of a democratic type -- of the civic type especially at the time that it was already clear that the Serbs had conducted an aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina and one could feel in the air that Ravno would not be the last place of attack but that we could expect many more. So in the eve of the war, which according to what had happened in Vukovar, could be expected to be worse and more serious, it was an illusion to speak about peaceful solutions while warmongering was going on, and it was [indiscernible] to accept an unitary concept of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I presented them with my views, my concept of a decentralised Bosnia and Herzegovina, and during the political negotiations which were supposed to be led by Mr. Kljujic and others who occupied even higher political and administrative posts than myself, I advocated the position that it was necessary to clearly articulate the position of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, because that segment of the population in Bosnia and Herzegovina, both during the old Yugoslavia and the socialist Yugoslavia was marginalised and discriminated against. After the democratic elections which were given the kind of support as they were, I expressed my position to Mr. Kljujic that the electorate which in -- which -- in large percentages voted for the HDZ, that he should expect a different kind of political attitude, a different kind of political behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And Mr. Maric, was your opinion shared by many of the party members from the Herceg-Bosna region, your political views on this?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: I cannot speak about percentages, but I can tell you my personal opinion. Also I think I can tell you what my impression was and what my knowledge at the time was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm going to interrupt you because the question was quite clear. I mean, were the party members from the Herceg-Bosna region, did they share your view? That was the question and I think you should try to answer a bit more summarily if possible, also for the time considerations.

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: I will. First of all, the Croatian Democratic Union, the Croatian Community of -- the HDZ did only concern the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna in at that meeting in Siroki Brijeg. The meeting was attended by the representatives of the party coming from Bihac, Banja Luka, Tuzla, that is the area which went beyond the boundaries of HDZ HB. Obviously, the views expressed differed. However, for the most part, and which would later become apparent at various congresses of the party, was against -- that they were against the concept which was advocated by Mr. Kljujic, a concept which I myself opposed as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Isn't it true, Mr. Maric, that during that meeting, several Bosnian Croats and I'm talking about the ones from the Herceg-Bosna region openly accused Stjepan Kljujic for being a traitor of the Croatian interests because he cooperated with the Muslim parties and brought the Croats into an inferior position? Isn't that the type of accusations that were made to Mr. Kljujic?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: That was a political debate, which had a certain amount of emotional impact and influence. Very often the words themselves, the heat of the discussion, could also be inappropriate or exaggerated. However, Mr. Kljujic remained in his position of the president of the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As for disagreements and differences, they remained within the framework of a political debate or discussion, and the same goes for Mr. Kljujic and myself. However, you're not right when you say that this was a problem which involved disagreements as to the positions of the HDZ and Kljujic's position towards other political parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Bosnian population in general. We were very clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'd like to make one more statement on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Because isn't it true that in this political debate that you were having in Siroki Brijeg that you literally said to Mr. Kljujic that the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina refused to be ruled by the Turks for another 500 years? Are those your literal words said at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to know about the foundation for this question. Is Mr. Bos reading from a document? Does he have any specific document or a transcript from the meeting? Where do these questions spring from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, we come across this issue many times. I believe that the Prosecution, in his cross-examination, will ask a question to this witness. If the witness did not remember what he said, then the Prosecution will furnish a document to refresh his memory. Let's hear the witness first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me remind you that I was not in the same position during my cross-examinations. I was required to provide the same explanation. I will prepare myself. I will read the transcript, and I will compose a written motion containing references to all your relevant decisions, as to the behaviour of the parties during the cross-examination, especially in view of the fact that we are receiving documents at the last notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your point will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will expose my views in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your point will be taken but we have to hear the witness first.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, could you answer my question? Did you say that the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina refused to be ruled by the Turks tore another 500 years at that meeting in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: JOZO Witness L
utterances.text: I know that I was very emotional during that meeting. You have to take into account my profession. I'm an art historian. I know very well who lives in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I know that no Turks live in Bosnia-Herzegovina but Croats, Bosniaks and Serbs. So at the heat of the debate, I may have used emotional language but I should like to have the transcript. It was not customary for me to communicate in this manner during such meetings. It was customary for me at all to offend the Muslim people and to use derogatory terms and I also hold in deep respects the Turkish people as well. I'm aware of the nuances. I'm aware of the sensitivity of the language and I should be reminded exactly of what happened on the 2nd of February if I'm not mistaken in 1992. Is that -- is that the date that you or, rather, the meeting that you had in mind? So ten years down the road, I think that I can speak about the atmosphere in general but I cannot be required to recall the specific language that I allegedly used and that you are now quoting in such express terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I will leave it there for now, Your Honour. Maybe just for counsel, this is taken from the transcript of Stjepan Kljujic which is one of our transcript witnesses and he's referring to this meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, Your Honours, that I am right in my position. It would have been appropriate for the Prosecutor to lay the relevant foundation and say that Mr. Kljujic, in his testimony, said words to the effect so and so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall refrain from any further comment. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Me too. Me neither will say anything about that. We are five minutes over the time. Witness, I'm afraid we have to keep you over the weekend here in The Hague and I have to warn you, as I did to other witnesses, that you are still under the oath during this period, so do not talk to anybody about your testimony and do not let anybody talk to you about it. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will resume next Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: be reconvened on Monday, the 15th day of April, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
